paragraphs.text: My kinsman and I were on our way back to Calcutta after a tour of the country in the Puja holidays when we met the Babu on the train. From his dress and appearance I took him at first for a Muslim from the western provinces. His talk only puzzled us further. He discussed every subject on earth in such a way that one would have thought the Maker of the universe consulted him first before doing anything at all. We had been living in perfect unconcern, knowing nothing of the unheard-of and secret things that were going on in the hidden workings of the world: that the Russians had advanced so far, that the English had such covert schemes, that a regular hotchpotch was coming to the boil among the native princes. Our new acquaintance smiled slightly and said, There happen more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are reported in your newspapers. This was the first time we had left home, and the man’s manner left us dumbfounded. On the slightest pretext he would talk science one moment and expound the Vedas the next, and then all of a sudden start reciting Persian couplets; and since we had no command whatever of science, the Vedas or the Persian tongue, our reverence for him grew by the hour. Indeed my kinsman, who was a Theosophist, became firmly convinced that our fellow traveller had some connection or other with the supernatural: some rare magnetism, or divine power, or subtle body, or something of that sort. He listened to even the most ordinary remarks of this extraordinary man in a rapt and reverent daze, and took notes on the quiet. I had the impression that the extraordinary person had quietly noticed this too, and was rather pleased.

When the train came in to the junction and stopped, we gathered in the waiting room to wait for the connecting train. It was then half past ten at night. We heard that because of some obstruction on the way the train would be very late. I had meanwhile decided to spread my bedding on the table and go to sleep, when that extraordinary person settled down and spun the following story. I got no more sleep that night.

Having differed over one or two matters of administration, I gave up my post in Junagadh and entered the service of the Nizam’s government in Hyderabad; and finding me young and robust, they straightaway put me to collecting the cotton duty at Barich.

Barich is a lovely spot. Below the lonely hills, through great forests, the little river Shusta (a corruption of the Sanskrit Svacchatoya, “clear-watered”) goes dancing swiftly on its way over a pebble-chattering bed, turning and bending at every step like an accomplished dancer. Right on the bank of that river, at the head of a towering ghat of a hundred and fifty stone-paved steps, a palace of white marble stands alone at the foot of the hills; there is no habitation anywhere near. The cotton market and the village of Barich lie far away from it.

Some two hundred and fifty years ago Shah Mahmud the Second had built the palace in this solitary place for his pleasures. In those days streams of rose-scented water would leap from the mouths of the fountains in its bath-house, and in that secluded chamber, cool with spray, young Persian women would sit on smooth marble-inlaid seats, stretch their soft bare feet into the clear water of the pool, loosen their hair before bathing, and with sitars in their laps sing ghazals of the vineyards.

Now those fountains play no longer, those songs are gone, no lovely white feet fall softly on the white stone; now it is the enormous and utterly empty lodging of a duty-collector like me, oppressed by solitude and without a companion. But Karim Khan, the old clerk at the office, had warned me again and again not to live in this palace. He had said, stay there by day if you wish, but never spend the night there. I laughed it off. The servants said they would work until evening but would not stay there at night. I said, so be it. The house had so evil a name that even thieves dared not come there at night.

When I first came, the desolation of this deserted stone palace seemed to press upon my chest like a dreadful weight. I stayed out as much as I could, working without a pause, and at night I came home and slept with a tired body.

But before a week had passed a strange intoxication from the house began, little by little, to lay siege to me. My condition then is hard to describe, and hard to make anyone believe. The whole house, like a living creature, seemed to be slowly digesting me in the enchanting juices of its belly.
Perhaps the process had begun the moment I set foot in the house; but I clearly remember the day on which I first consciously felt it begin.

It was the start of summer and the market was slack; I had no work on hand. A little before sunset I had taken an easy chair down to the lowest landing of the ghat by the river and was sitting there. The Shusta had dwindled by then; on the far side a wide stretch of sandbank had taken on the colours of the late afternoon light, and on this side, at the foot of the steps, the pebbles glinted and glittered under the clear shallow water. There was no wind anywhere that day. From the thickets of wild basil, mint and fennel on the nearby hills a heavy fragrance rose and hung like a burden on the motionless sky.

The instant the sun sank behind the hilltop, a long curtain of shadow dropped over the theatre of the day; here, with the hills in the way, the meeting of light and darkness at sunset does not last long. I was on the point of getting up, meaning to go out for a quick gallop, when I heard footsteps on the stairs. I turned and looked behind me: there was no one.

I took it for a trick of the senses and turned back to sit down again, and at once I heard a great many footsteps together, as if a crowd were running and racing down the stairs. A strange thrill, mixed with a little fear, filled my whole body. Though there was no figure in front of me, it seemed as clear to me as if I saw it with my eyes that on this summer evening a band of pleasure-loving, restless women had come down to bathe in the waters of the Shusta. Though in that evening hour there was not the faintest sound anywhere, on the silent hillside, on the riverbank or in the empty palace, I seemed to hear plainly the bathers going past me, chasing one another with laughter as playful as a hundred streams of a waterfall. They did not seem to notice me. As they were invisible to me, so I seemed to be invisible to them. The river was as still as before, yet I felt distinctly that the shallow current of the clear-watered stream was being stirred into turmoil by many arms flung out with a jingle of bangles; that the companions, laughing and laughing, were splashing water over one another; and that the swimmers’ kicking feet were flinging the drops into the air like handfuls of pearls.

A kind of trembling began in my breast; whether the excitement was of fear, or of joy, or of curiosity, I cannot rightly say. I longed to look properly, but there was nothing in front of me to see; I felt that if I only listened carefully I would hear everything they said quite clearly, but when I listened with all my mind I heard only the crickets of the forest. It seemed to me that a black curtain two hundred and fifty years old was swaying just in front of me; I would lift one edge in fear and trembling and peer inside, and there a great assembly was gathered, but in the thick darkness nothing could be seen.

Suddenly the sultry stillness broke and a wind came rushing; before my eyes the still surface of the Shusta rippled up like the tresses of a nymph, and the whole forest, wrapped in evening shadow, broke into a rustle all at once, as if it were waking from a nightmare. Call it a dream or call it the truth: the invisible mirage that had come down before me, cast back from a field of the past two hundred and fifty years away, vanished in a flash. The phantom women who had run past me with swift bodiless feet and loud soundless laughter and leapt into the waters of the Shusta did not come back up past me wringing the water from the ends of their wet garments. As the wind carries off a fragrance, so they were carried away on a single breath of spring.

Then a great fear seized me that the goddess of poetry, finding me alone, had suddenly come to possess me, perched on my shoulders; that I, a poor wretch who earns his bread by the drudgery of collecting the cotton duty, was now to have my head taken by that destroyer of men. I thought I must eat a good meal; it is on an empty stomach that every kind of incurable disease comes and takes hold. I called my cook and ordered a proper Mughlai dinner, rich with ghee and fragrant with spices.

Next morning the whole business seemed supremely ridiculous. Absently, wearing a sola topi like a sahib and driving my carriage with my own hands, I rattled off to my inspection work. That day was the day for writing my quarterly report, so I was expected home late. But even before evening had properly come on, something began to pull me towards the house. Who was pulling me I cannot say; but I felt it was not right to delay any longer. I felt they were all sitting waiting. Leaving the report unfinished, I put the sola topi on my head and, startling with the rattle of my wheels that lonely road, grey with dusk and dense with the shade of trees, I arrived at the huge, silent, dark palace standing at the edge of the hills.

At the top of the stairs the front room was immense. Carved arches resting on three rows of great pillars held up its broad roof. This enormous room hummed day and night with the weight of its own vast emptiness. That day, at the approach of evening, the lamps had not yet been lit. As soon as I pushed open the door and entered that great room, it seemed as though a tremendous upheaval had broken out within it; as though an assembly had suddenly broken up, and through the doors, windows, rooms, passages and verandas on every side people had fled, there was no telling who had gone which way. Seeing nothing anywhere, I stood there astonished. My body thrilled with a kind of rapture. It was as if the faint scent of hair-oils and attar, the lingering remains of long-ago days, began to steal into my nostrils. Standing among the rows of ancient stone columns in that vast, lampless, deserted room, I heard the fountains’ water splashing down on the white stone; a sitar playing some tune I could not make out; here the tinkle of golden ornaments, there the chime of anklets; now and then the hour struck on a great copper gong; very far off, the opening strains of the nahabat; the tinkling of the crystal drops of a chandelier swaying in the breeze; the song of caged bulbuls from the veranda; the call of tame cranes from the garden: all around me they began to weave a raga of the world of ghosts.

Such an enchantment came over me that it seemed this untouchable, unreachable, unreal affair was the one truth in the world, and all else a false mirage. That I was I, that is to say, that I was Sriyukta So-and-so, eldest son of So-and-so, who drew a salary of four hundred and fifty rupees for collecting the cotton duty; that I went to office in a sola topi and short coat driving a tum-tum: all this seemed to me so strange, so laughable, so baseless a lie, that standing in the middle of that vast, silent, dark room I burst into loud laughter.

At that very moment my Muslim servant came into the room carrying a lighted kerosene lamp. Whether or not he thought me mad I do not know, but at once I remembered that I was indeed Sriyukta So-and-so Nath, eldest son of the late So-and-so Chandra; and I reflected too that whether, somewhere within the world or outside it, bodiless fountains play for all eternity and endless ragas sound on some magic sitar at the touch of invisible fingers, only our great poets and their eminent fellows can say; but this much is certainly true, that I collect the cotton duty at the Barich market and draw a salary of four hundred and fifty rupees a month. Then, remembering my strange enchantment of a moment before, I took up the newspaper beside my camp table in the light of the kerosene lamp and laughed with amusement.

When I had read the newspaper and eaten my Mughlai dinner, I put out the lamp in a small corner room and lay down in bed. Through the open window in front of me, above the dark, forest-girdled heights of the Arali hills, a single brilliant star gazed steadily from a sky millions of leagues away at Sriyukta Duty-Collector on his paltry camp bed; and while I felt wonder and amusement at this, I fell asleep, I cannot say when. Nor do I know how long I slept. All at once I woke with a shudder. It was not that there had been any sound in the room, nor could I see that anyone had come in. The unwinking star had set behind the dark hill, and the faint light of the waning moon had come in at my window, pale and shrinking, as if it knew it had no right to be there.

I saw no one at all, and yet I felt quite distinctly that someone was gently pushing me. As soon as I woke, she said not a word, but simply seemed to beckon with her five ringed fingers, bidding me follow her with the utmost care.

I got up very, very quietly. Though in that vast palace of a hundred chambers, of huge emptiness, of sleeping sounds and wakeful echoes, there was not a living soul besides myself, at every step I was afraid that someone might wake. Most of the rooms in the palace were kept shut, and I had never once been into them.

Where I was going that night, following with soundless steps and held breath that invisible summoner, I cannot say clearly today. How many narrow dark passages, how many long verandas, how many solemn, silent, enormous halls of audience, how many small, airless, secret chambers I went through, there is no reckoning.

Though I could not see my invisible messenger with my eyes, her form was not hidden from my mind. An Arab woman: through her loose hanging sleeves showed arms firm and smoothly rounded as if carved from white marble; from the edge of her cap a veil of fine cloth fell over her face; and at her waist a curved dagger was fastened.

It seemed to me that one of the thousand and one nights of the Arabian Nights had flown out of the world of stories tonight. It was as if, in the dark of midnight, I had set out through the narrow, lampless streets of sleeping Baghdad on some perilous lovers’ errand.

At last my messenger stopped short before a curtain of deep blue and seemed to point downward with her finger. There was nothing there below, but the blood in my breast froze with fear. I sensed that on the floor in front of that curtain a fearsome African eunuch dressed in brocade sat with his legs stretched out, a naked sword across his lap, nodding and dozing. The messenger stepped lightly over his two legs and lifted one corner of the curtain.

Inside, part of a room spread with a Persian carpet came into view. Who sat upon the divan could not be seen; I saw only, below the hems of full saffron-coloured trousers, two small and lovely feet in gold-embroidered slippers, resting idly on a rose-pink velvet cushion. On one side of the floor, in a bluish crystal bowl, apples, pears, oranges and many bunches of grapes were set out, and beside it two little cups and a decanter of golden wine stood waiting for a guest. From inside the room an intoxicating fragrant smoke of some rare incense drifted out and overwhelmed my senses.
With trembling heart I was just stepping over the eunuch’s outstretched legs when he started awake, and the sword slid off his lap and fell with a clatter on the stone floor.

Suddenly, startled by a hideous shriek, I found myself sitting on my camp bed bathed in sweat; in the light of dawn the broken moon of the dark fortnight had turned pale like a sick man worn out by a sleepless night; and our mad Meher Ali, as was his daily custom, was going along the deserted road at daybreak, shouting, “Tafat jao! Tafat jao! Stand back! Stand back!”
Thus my one night of the Arabian Nights came abruptly to an end; but a thousand nights still remained.

A great quarrel now broke out between my days and my nights. By day I went to my work weary and spent, and kept cursing the night, that bewitching sorceress full of empty dreams; and again, after dusk, my daytime existence, bound to its work, seemed utterly trivial, false and absurd.

After dusk I would be caught up, bewildered, in a net of intoxication. I would become another, a strange person, belonging to some unwritten history of hundreds of years ago; then the short English coat and tight trousers no longer suited me. Then I would put a red velvet fez on my head, put on loose pyjamas, a flowered kaba and a long silk choga, perfume a coloured handkerchief with attar, and dress with great care; and throwing away my cigarette, I would take up a great albola of many coils filled with rose-water and seat myself in a large high-cushioned chair, as though I were waiting with eager longing for some wonderful meeting with a beloved in the night.

After that, as the darkness thickened, what a strange thing would begin to happen I cannot describe. It was exactly as though some torn fragments of a marvellous story were being blown about by a sudden spring wind through the many curious rooms of this great palace. One could follow them a little way, and after that the end was nowhere to be seen. And I too, pursuing those whirling, scattered fragments, would wander from room to room the whole night through.

In this whirlpool of broken dreams, amid these waves of air, here a scent of henna, there a sound of a sitar, here a breeze laden with fragrant spray, I would catch sight of a heroine, now and again, for an instant, like a flash of lightning. It was she who wore the saffron-coloured trousers, and on her two soft feet, white flushed with red, gold-embroidered slippers with curling toes; a tight-fitting bodice worked with flowers in gold thread was fastened over her breast; on her head was a red cap, and from it a golden fringe hung down to encircle her white forehead and cheeks.

She had driven me mad. In pursuit of her I have roamed night after night, lane by lane and chamber by chamber, through the enchanted city of dreams, tangled with winding ways, in the underworld kingdom of sleep.

Some evenings, while I was dressing myself with care like a prince before the big mirror, with a candle lit on either side of it, I would suddenly see the shadow of that young Iranian woman fall for an instant beside my reflection in the glass; in the twinkling of an eye she would turn her neck, cast from the large, deep-black pupils of her eyes a glance of profound, passionate, anguished longing, give on her full and lovely lips, red as the bimba fruit, only the faint hint of some unspoken word, whirl her body, a vine in the flower of youth, swiftly upward in a light and graceful dance, and, showering in a single moment sparks of pain, desire and bewitchment, of laughter, glances and glittering jewels, melt away into the mirror itself. A wild gust of wind, plundering all the fragrances of the hills and woods, would come and blow out my two candles; I would leave off my dressing and lie down on the bed at the far end of the dressing-room, my body thrilling and my eyes closed; and all around me, in that wind, in all the mingled perfumes of the Arali hill-groves, many caresses, many kisses, many tender touches of hands seemed to come and roam about, filling the secluded darkness; I would hear many soft murmurs close to my ear; a fragrant breath would fall upon my forehead; and a soft orna, delicately and delightfully scented, would come fluttering again and again to brush my cheek. Little by little an enchanting serpent seemed to bind my whole body in her intoxicating coils; heaving a deep sigh, I would sink, numb and senseless, into the deepest sleep.

One afternoon I made up my mind to go out riding. Someone, I do not know who, kept forbidding me, but that day I would not heed the prohibition. My English hat and short coat were hanging on a wooden peg; I had taken them down and was about to put them on, when suddenly a violent whirlwind, raising banners of sand from the Shusta and of dry leaves from the Arali hills, swept that coat and hat away, spinning them round and round; and a peal of exceedingly sweet laughter, whirling round and round with the wind, striking every note in the scale of mirth one after another, rose from octave to higher octave until it faded away near the realm of the setting sun.
There was no riding that day, and from the day after I gave up wearing that comical short coat and English hat altogether.

And that same night, in the dead of night, I sat up in bed and heard someone weeping as though dying, sobbing and sobbing in stifled moans, as if her heart would burst; as though from beneath my bed, beneath the floor, from inside a damp, dark grave below the stone foundations of this great palace, she were crying and crying out: Take me away, rescue me; break through all the doors of hard enchantment, of deep sleep, of fruitless dreams; lift me onto your horse, hold me close against your breast, and carry me through the forest, over the hills, across the river, into your sunlit rooms! Rescue me!

Who am I? How can I rescue you! Out of this whirling, ever-changing stream of dreams, what drowning beauty of desire am I to drag to the shore! When were you, and where were you, O heavenly one! Beside what cool spring, in the shade of what grove of date palms, in the lap of what homeless daughter of the desert were you born! What Bedouin robber tore you from your mother’s arms as one plucks a bud from a forest creeper, set you on a horse as swift as lightning, crossed the burning sands, and carried you off to be sold in the slave market of what royal city! There what servant of what emperor, gazing on the shy and trembling beauty of your newly blossomed youth, counted out gold coins for you, carried you over the sea seated in a golden palanquin, and presented you to the inner apartments of his master’s house! And there, what a history! Amid the music of the sarangi, the chime of anklets and the golden wine of Shiraz, now and again the flash of a dagger, the burning of poison, the wound of a glance! What boundless splendour, what endless prison! On either side two slave girls wave the chamar, lightning flashing from the diamonds of their bangles; the Shahenshah, king of kings, lies grovelling beside the jewelled, pearl-studded slippers beneath your white feet; outside the door, like the messenger of Death, stands the Habshi, dressed like an angel, a naked sword in his hand. And then, swept along on that blood-stained, jealousy-foaming, intrigue-ridden stream of dreadful, dazzling splendour, into what cruel death did you sink, O flower-spray of the desert, or upon what yet crueller shore of glory were you cast?

Just then that mad Meher Ali suddenly cried out: “Stand back, stand back! Sab jhut hai, sab jhut hai! It is all false, all false!” I looked and saw that it was morning; the chaprasi brought the letters from the post and put them in my hand, and the cook came, made his salaam, and asked what kind of dinner was to be prepared that day.

I said, no, I can stay in this house no longer. That very day I packed up my belongings and moved into the office building. The old clerk at the office, Karim Khan, smiled slightly when he saw me. Annoyed by his smile, I made him no answer and set to work.

The nearer the afternoon drew on towards evening, the more absent-minded I grew; I felt there was somewhere I had to go at once; the work of examining the cotton accounts seemed altogether needless, and even the Nizam’s government seemed of no great account to me; everything that was present, everything that was moving and turning and toiling and eating around me, seemed utterly poor, meaningless and insignificant.

I flung down my pen, shut the big ledger, got into my tum-tum at once and drove off. I found that the tum-tum stopped of its own accord, at the very moment of dusk, at the door of that stone palace. I ran swiftly up the steps and went inside.

Today all was silent. The dark rooms seemed to be sulking, their faces heavy with anger. My heart began to overflow with remorse, but I could find no one to tell, no one to beg forgiveness from. With an empty heart I wandered about from one dark room to another. I longed to take some instrument in my hands and sing to someone, saying: O flame! The moth that tried to fly away and leave you has come back to die. Forgive it this time; burn up both its wings, reduce it to ashes!

Suddenly two drops of tears fell on my forehead from above. That day dense, dark clouds had gathered on the peaks of the Arali hills. The dark forest and the ink-black water of the Shusta had grown still in a dreadful expectancy. Water, earth and sky suddenly shuddered; and all at once a storm, baring its teeth of lightning, came rushing through the distant pathless forest like a madman who has broken his chains, shrieking in anguish. The great empty rooms of the palace slammed all their doors and wailed aloud in bitter pain.

Today the servants were all at the office; there was no one here to light the lamps. On that cloudy, moonless night, in the pitch-black darkness inside the house, I could distinctly feel a woman lying face down on the carpet at the foot of the bed, tearing at her loosened hair with both fists tightly clenched; blood was bursting from her fair forehead; now she broke into a dry, harsh, wild laugh, now she sobbed and sobbed as though she would burst; with both hands she tore the bodice from her breast and beat her bare breast; the wind came roaring in at the open window, and the rain poured down in torrents and drenched her whole body.

All night long neither the storm stopped nor the weeping. In fruitless remorse I went wandering from room to room in the dark. There was no one anywhere; whom was I to console? Whose was this fierce, wounded pride? From where was this restless lamentation rising?
The madman cried out, “Stand back, stand back! It is all false, it is all false!”

I saw that dawn had come, and that Meher Ali, even on this day of dreadful storm, was going round the palace as usual and raising his customary cry. It suddenly struck me that perhaps this Meher Ali too had once lived in this palace as I did, and that now, though he had come out of it mad, he was still drawn by the spell of this stone demon to come every day at daybreak and go round it.
At once I ran through the rain to the madman and asked him, “Meher Ali, what is it that is false?”

He gave no answer to my question but pushed me aside and went round and round the house, shrieking, like a bird spellbound, circling about the jaws of a python. Only, as though struggling with all his might to warn himself, he kept saying over and over, “Stand back, stand back! It is all false, it is all false!”
Like a madman, through the storm and rain, I went to the office, called Karim Khan and said to him, Tell me plainly what this means.

The substance of what the old man said was this: once, in that palace, many unsated longings, many flames of frenzied pleasure had blazed and surged; and from all that burning of hearts, from the curse of all those fruitless desires, every stone of the palace has become hungry and thirsty, and whenever it finds a living man it longs to devour him like a slavering she-demon. Of all who had lived three nights in that palace, only Meher Ali had come out, and he had lost his mind; no one else to this day had escaped its jaws.
I asked, Is there no way at all for me to be saved?

The old man said, There is one way only, and it is very hard. I shall tell it to you; but before that I must tell the old history of an Iranian slave girl of that Gulbagh. Never in this world has anything happened so strange or so heartbreaking.

Just then the porters came to say that the train was coming. So soon? While we were hastily strapping up our bedding, the train came in. In its first class an Englishman, just roused from sleep, was leaning out of the window trying to read the name of the station; the moment he saw our travelling companion he called out “Hallo!” and took him into his own carriage. We got into the second class. We never learnt who the Babu was, nor did we hear the end of the story.
I said, The fellow took us for fools and hoaxed us for his amusement; the story was made up from beginning to end.
Over this dispute my Theosophist kinsman and I have parted for the rest of our lives.
